clinicalScope: Thrombosis (arterial and venous) in adult patients presenting to low‑resource hospitals in East Africa and similar settings
title: Thrombosis
subject: Pathology
summary: Thrombosis is a clot that blocks a blood vessel, stopping blood flow. In East African hospitals it often follows infection, immobility, or pregnancy and can cause limb loss, stroke, or death if not recognised quickly.

sections.p: Thrombosis is the pathological formation of a fibrin‑rich clot (thrombus) inside a vessel, obstructing flow. It is classified by location (arterial vs venous) and by acute vs chronic presentation.
b: Arterial thrombosis: platelet‑rich, high shear, often on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque.
Venous thrombosis: fibrin‑rich, low shear, frequently in deep veins of the leg or splanchnic veins.
Mixed (arterial‑venous) thrombosis can occur in trauma or central lines.
Acute thrombosis presents with sudden ischemia; chronic thrombosis may cause collateral formation.

sections.p: Risk factors follow Virchow’s triad – endothelial injury, stasis, and hypercoagulability – with local modifiers in low‑resource settings.
b: Endothelial injury: atherosclerosis, malaria‑related vasculitis, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion, trauma, central venous catheters.
Stasis: prolonged bed rest, postpartum immobilisation, heart failure, long‑haul travel, varicose veins.
Hypercoagulability: HIV infection, active tuberculosis, malignancy, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias.
Environmental: dehydration from diarrhoeal disease, herbal remedies containing estrogenic compounds.

sections.p: Clot formation proceeds through a cascade of cellular and molecular events that differ between arteries and veins.
b: Endothelial disruption exposes sub‑endothelial collagen → platelet adhesion via von Willebrand factor.
Platelet activation releases ADP and thromboxane A2 → aggregation and formation of a platelet plug (arterial).
Tissue factor exposure triggers the extrinsic coagulation pathway → thrombin generation → fibrin polymerisation (venous).
Thrombin amplifies its own production (positive feedback) and stabilises the clot with factor XIII cross‑linking.

sections.p: The appearance of a thrombus varies with age and vessel type.
b: White (platelet‑rich) thrombus: firm, pale, adherent to arterial wall.
Red (fibrin‑rich) thrombus: gelatinous, dark, often occluding venous lumen.
Mixed thrombus: layered appearance (lines of Zahn) indicating alternating platelet‑rich and fibrin‑rich layers.
Chronic thrombus: organized, firm, may show recanalisation channels.

sections.p: Histology reveals the composition and age of the clot.
b: Lines of Zahn: alternating pale platelet layers and dark fibrin‑RBC layers – hallmark of antemortem arterial thrombus.
Red cell‑rich fibrin meshwork with few platelets – typical of venous thrombus.
Endothelial overgrowth and neovascularisation in chronic organised thrombus.
Inflammatory infiltrates (neutrophils, macrophages) indicate recent formation.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ supplied by the occluded vessel and the speed of occlusion.
b: Arterial: sudden, severe pain, pallor, pulselessness, cold limb (acute limb ischemia); stroke – focal neurological deficit; myocardial infarction – crushing chest pain.
Venous: swelling, pain, warmth, and tenderness along a deep vein (DVT); abdominal pain, ascites, splenomegaly in portal vein thrombosis.
Systemic: fever, tachycardia, and signs of embolisation (e.g., pulmonary embolism causing dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain).
Chronic: collateral circulation may mask symptoms but can cause chronic venous insufficiency or post‑thrombotic syndrome.

sections.p: Select tests that answer the key clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there a thrombus in a superficial or deep vein? – Compressibility loss, echogenic intraluminal material, colour flow obstruction; if unavailable, use clinical Wells score + D‑dimer.
Is there active fibrin degradation suggesting recent clot? – Elevated >500 µg/L FEU supports DVT/PE in low‑pretest probability; a normal result can rule out in low‑risk patients.
Is there a pulmonary embolus? – Filling defect in pulmonary artery; if CT unavailable, use bedside echocardiography for right‑ventricular strain.
Is myocardial infarction present? – ST‑segment changes, troponin rise; if labs unavailable, rely on clinical chest pain pattern and ECG.
Is there a coagulopathy that may affect treatment? – Prolonged PT/INR suggests liver disease; low fibrinogen may indicate consumptive coagulopathy.

sections.p: Severity guides urgency of therapy and monitoring.
b: Arterial: Rutherford classification for acute limb ischemia (class I–III based on viability).
Venous: Wells score (low, moderate, high) predicts pre‑test probability; CEAP classification for chronic venous disease.
Pulmonary embolism: PESI (Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index) or simplified PESI to stratify mortality risk.
Portal vein thrombosis: acute vs chronic; presence of bowel ischemia defines high‑risk.

sections.p: Complications arise from the clot itself or from treatment.
b: Arterial embolisation → stroke, myocardial infarction, organ infarction.
Venous embolisation → pulmonary embolism, right‑heart strain, death.
Post‑thrombotic syndrome: chronic pain, swelling, ulceration after DVT.
Bleeding from anticoagulation, especially in patients with malaria‑related thrombocytopenia or hepatic dysfunction.

sections.p: Management balances rapid clot control with bleeding risk, using drugs and, when feasible, procedural options.
b: Anticoagulation is first‑line for most venous thromboses: unfractionated heparin (IV) or low‑molecular‑weight heparin (sub‑Q) if available; switch to warfarin for long‑term therapy.
In arterial occlusion, urgent reperfusion: thrombolysis (streptokinase, alteplase) if fibrinolytic agents are stocked, or surgical embolectomy/angioplasty where expertise exists.
Compression stockings and early mobilisation to prevent DVT recurrence.
Treat underlying cause: anti‑TB therapy, antiretroviral therapy, malaria treatment, control of diabetes and hypertension.

sections.p: Linking morphology to bedside findings helps the examiner.
b: Lines of Zahn on histology explain why arterial clots cause abrupt, severe ischemia.
Red‑cell‑rich venous thrombus correlates with gradual limb swelling and positive Homans sign.
Organised chronic thrombus with collateral veins accounts for mild symptoms despite large occlusion.
Elevated D‑dimer reflects fibrin turnover, useful when imaging is delayed.

sections.p: A systematic bedside and investigative plan maximises marks.
b: History: onset, pain quality, risk factors (immobility, infection, pregnancy, drugs).
Examination: inspect for colour change, palpate pulses, perform Homan’s sign, assess for leg swelling, check for neurological deficits.
First test: bedside Doppler or Wells score + D‑dimer; if positive, start anticoagulation while arranging imaging.
Escalation: if limb is cold, pulseless, and motor loss present → immediate reperfusion (thrombolysis or surgery).
Follow‑up: monitor INR if on warfarin, assess for bleeding, educate on compression and activity.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of pulse or motor function in a limb
Severe chest pain radiating to arm or jaw
Acute dyspnoea with pleuritic chest pain

faq.q: Why are arterial clots platelet‑rich while venous clots are fibrin‑rich?
faq.a: High shear stress in arteries activates platelets quickly; low shear in veins favours the coagulation cascade and fibrin formation.
Severe malaria can trigger endothelial activation and dehydration, both of which increase stasis and hypercoagulability.

faq.q: What if ultrasound is not available for suspected DVT?
faq.a: Use a validated clinical probability score (Wells) plus D‑dimer; if high probability, start anticoagulation empirically.

exam: A 28‑year‑old postpartum woman presents with unilateral calf swelling and pain. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Apply Wells score, obtain D‑dimer; if high probability start anticoagulation while arranging duplex ultrasound.
Explain how lines of Zahn help differentiate antemortem from post‑mortem clots. — Presence of alternating pale and dark layers indicates formation in flowing blood, confirming antemortem thrombosis.

A patient with sickle cell disease develops acute chest pain and a cold foot. Which type of thrombosis is most likely and what immediate therapy is indicated? — Arterial thrombosis causing acute limb ischemia; urgent reperfusion with thrombolysis or embolectomy.
Why is unfractionated heparin preferred over LMWH in a patient with severe renal impairment? — UFH is cleared renally independent and can be rapidly reversed with protamine.

List three hypercoagulable conditions common in East Africa and how they modify management. — HIV (monitor drug interactions), active TB (ensure anti‑TB drugs before warfarin), malaria‑induced dehydration (aggressive fluid replacement).
Interpret a D‑dimer of 800 µg/L in a low‑risk patient with leg pain. — Despite elevation, low pre‑test probability makes false‑positive likely; consider alternative diagnoses before anticoagulation.

What are the key components of the Rutherford classification for acute limb ischemia? — Viability (class I), threatened (class IIa/IIb), irreversible (class III) based on sensory/motor loss and Doppler signals.

Describe the management hierarchy for a massive pulmonary embolism in a setting without thrombolytics. — Initiate UFH, consider surgical embolectomy if available, provide supportive oxygen and haemodynamic support.
How does compression therapy reduce recurrence of DVT? — Increases venous velocity, reduces stasis, and promotes valve function.
A patient on warfarin develops a sudden rise in INR to 6.0. What steps do you take? — Hold warfarin, give vitamin K if bleeding risk high, monitor INR until therapeutic range restored.
